pages.x: It began with a quarrel over who held the keys of the Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem: Catholic monks backed by France, or Orthodox ones backed by Russia. Behind it lay a bigger question: who would gain as the Ottoman Empire, the sick man of Europe, grew weaker. In 1853 Russia marched into Ottoman lands on the Danube.

In November 1853 a Russian fleet caught Ottoman ships in the harbour of Sinop on the Black Sea and destroyed them with new exploding shells, killing some 3,000 men. Britain and France, fearing that Russia would take Constantinople, declared war in March 1854.

pages.t: The Charge of the Light Brigade
pages.x: The allies landed in Crimea to take Sevastopol, Russia's great naval base. At Balaklava in October 1854 a muddled order sent some 670 British light cavalry straight down a valley into Russian guns on three sides. Within minutes over a third were killed, wounded or taken. A French general watching said it was magnificent, but it was not war.

pages.t: Theirs but to do and die
pages.x: The poet Alfred Tennyson read the report in The Times and wrote a poem, it is said, within minutes. Its lines about the six hundred riding into the valley of Death, theirs not to reason why, made the charge a legend of courage, and of the waste of it.
pages.img: The Charge of the Light Brigade (poem)

pages.x: Reports of wounded men dying in filth shocked Britain. Florence Nightingale took 38 nurses to the army hospital at Scutari, across from Constantinople. She fought the army for supplies, cleaned the wards and walked them at night with a lamp. Deaths fell sharply once the drains were fixed in 1855, and she used charts to prove why.

Mary Seacole, a Jamaican nurse and businesswoman, offered to join the army nurses and was turned away. She paid her own way to Crimea and built the British Hotel near Balaklava, selling food and supplies to officers and nursing wounded men, sometimes on the battlefield itself. Soldiers called her Mother Seacole.

The allies besieged Sevastopol for almost a year. Inside, a young Russian artillery officer, Leo Tolstoy, wrote sketches of the siege that made his name. In September 1855 the French stormed the Malakhov fort, and the Russians left the burning city. Tolstoy went on to write War and Peace.
William Howard Russell of The Times sent home some of the first reports from a front line, and Roger Fenton hauled a darkroom van around Crimea to take some of the first photographs of a war.
pages.fx: For the first time people at home learned within weeks what their soldiers suffered, and governments could no longer hide it.
pages.img: The Valley of the Shadow of Death (photograph)

pages.x: The war ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1856, which kept Russian warships out of the Black Sea. Perhaps half a million men died, far more of cholera and dysentery than of wounds. Defeat pushed the new tsar to free Russia's serfs in 1861, and Nightingale made nursing a respected profession.
